topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Make a requested action into an object that can be stored and invoked through a common operation. The sender then chooses when to trigger work without knowing its details. The EPUB motivates this with buttons, menus, and keyboard shortcuts that should share one action instead of duplicating editor logic.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Represent a delayed request with its arguments.
Explain successful execution and reverse-order undo.
Identify the lifetime and isolation conditions an undo mechanism needs.

blocks.text: A concrete command stores the receiver and arguments needed for a request. The client creates it; the invoker triggers it; the receiver performs the domain operation. A very small command may perform its own work. Delaying execution is distinct from undo: undo requires an additional policy and enough previous state to reverse the successful change.

cards.question: What is Command?
cards.answer: An object that stores a request and provides an operation to perform it.

cards.question: What is Receiver?
cards.answer: The object whose real state or service a command uses.

cards.question: What is Commit point?
cards.answer: The point after which an operation is recorded as successfully applied.

cards.question: What is Compensation?
cards.answer: A later action intended to offset an effect that cannot literally be undone.

cards.question: Does the supplied Command interface already provide undo?
cards.answer: No. It declares Execute only. Undo is a possible use of the pattern and needs extra state and operations.

cards.question: Why must the second Move capture three during execution?
cards.answer: Three is the receiver state immediately before its change. Capturing at construction would remember zero and skip the first move when undoing the second.

topics.title: The problem: moving a marker is easy until timing changes
topics.summary: A planning screen shows a marker at an integer position from zero through ten. Moving it immediately is simple: call marker.set(7). The setter rejects values outside the range and otherwise stores the new position. That direct call is the right first design when every request happens now and never needs undo. The new requirements are different: collect several moves, perform them later in order, and let the user undo that group in reverse order. The program must also reject a second execution of a move that is already applied.

blocks.text: A vector of destination integers can delay this one operation. However, if the screen later queues a rename or a color change, a vector of integers no longer describes all actions. A growing collection of parallel arrays for action codes and arguments is easy to misalign. The missing idea is to store a request together with the data and behavior needed to carry it out. That stored request is a command. We introduce an interface only because a single queue may need different kinds of requests with the same execute and undo operations.

topics.title: A command has intent before it has a history
topics.summary: Move stores a borrowed Marker reference and a target position. Its constructor records intent but does not move the marker. The reference means there is one actual marker: copying the marker into each command would create private markers and leave the screen unchanged. target_ is stored by value so a later change to a caller variable cannot silently change the queued destination. before_ becomes meaningful only when execute runs. Saving it during construction would record the wrong old position for the second command in a delayed queue.

blocks.text: The interface has virtual execute and undo functions, so callers can use a Command reference without knowing which concrete request it holds. A virtual destructor allows deletion through the base type. Move uses override to ask the compiler to confirm that its functions truly replace those interface functions. std::unique_ptr<Command> owns each queued command. The vector owns its smart pointers, while each command merely borrows the marker. In main the marker is declared before the queue and is destroyed after it, so all borrowed references remain valid.

topics.title: Execution has a commit point
topics.summary: Move begins with applied_ false. execute first rejects a repeated call. It then saves the current marker position, asks the marker to accept the target, and only after success sets applied_ true. This last step is a commit point: the flag now says there is a completed change that can be undone. If the setter rejects eleven, the marker remains unchanged and applied_ remains false. before_ may have been refreshed, but it does not authorize undo because the flag is still false.

blocks.text: This order is not cosmetic. Setting applied_ true before the setter succeeds would mark a failed request as part of the undo history. Updating the marker before validating the target would allow an invalid state even if an exception is thrown afterward. Here the setter validates first and then assigns one integer, which cannot throw. The program therefore gives a clear guarantee for a bad target: the visible marker stays as it was. This guarantee depends on the receiver behavior; a command cannot make a partly failing external service atomic merely by adding a bool.

topics.title: Undo reverses successful requests in reverse order
topics.summary: The first queued move records zero and sets three. The second records three and sets seven. To reverse the group, undo the second move to restore three, then undo the first to restore zero. The reverse iterators rbegin and rend traverse the vector from its last element toward its first. In (*it)->undo(), *it obtains the unique pointer stored at the iterator position; the arrow accesses the owned command. Iteration changes which command is selected, not who owns it.

blocks.text: An undo operation is permitted only for an applied command. After restoration, applied_ becomes false and another execute is allowed; that is the limited redo behavior of this implementation. Redo reads a new before_ value at execution time. It does not promise to replay the exact historical environment. The design assumes exclusive, ordered changes to this marker while a history is active. If unrelated code changes the marker to nine between execution and undo, blindly restoring before_ can erase that later change. Real editors often route all edits through one history owner or use version checks to detect conflicts.

topics.title: Queueing, undo, and transactions are separate promises
topics.summary: The primary queue loop runs commands in order but does not automatically undo earlier commands if a later one fails. A transaction is a group treated as one success or failure under a stated contract. The lab adds a small transaction runner for range failures: it counts successfully applied commands and reverses only that prefix. An empty batch succeeds without changing the marker. A batch containing targets six and eleven returns failure and restores the original zero. This works because the local receiver and undo operations have tightly controlled behavior.

blocks.text: A command can also represent an operation that cannot truly be undone. Sending a message may be followed by a correction, but the recipient may already have read it. A compensation is a new action that tries to offset an earlier effect; it is not time travel. Another option for local state is a snapshot, developed in Chapter 17, which remembers the state instead of how to reverse each action. For this marker, two integers and a flag are cheaper and clearer than a general snapshot system. Choose what must be preserved before promising undo to a user.

topics.title: Worked example: contracts and alternatives
topics.summary: An undoable queue of marker moves

blocks.title: Requirements
items: Keep marker positions within 0 through 10.
Construction must not execute a request.
Undo applied moves in reverse order and reject invalid command states.

blocks.text: Move holds the receiver, destination, prior position, and an applied flag. The queue owns commands but borrows no internal marker storage. Receiver validation happens before the command commits success.

blocks.title: Invariants
items: The marker stays within its allowed range.
Only successful executions set applied_ true.
Commands must not outlive their borrowed receiver.
Undo history assumes no unrelated edits to the receiver.

blocks.text: Alternative: A vector of integers with a loop is sufficient for a fixed set of move-only requests. A std::function<void()> queue is compact for delayed work, but an undo contract still needs saved state and pairing between forward and reverse behavior.

Verification: Checks cover delayed execution, the final queue value, repeated execution rejection, reverse undo, invalid destination, undo of a failed command, the upper boundary, and execute-after-undo. They do not establish persistence, concurrency safety, or recovery from process failure.

Maintenance: Representing requests explicitly gives a debugger a concrete place to inspect their arguments and state. Keep the history owner responsible for ordering and receiver lifetime instead of scattering undo calls across user-interface components.

workshop.title: An undoable queue of marker moves
workshop.problem: An undoable queue of marker moves. Keep marker positions within 0 through 10. Construction must not execute a request. Undo applied moves in reverse order and reject invalid command states.
workshop.output:
after queue: 7
after undo: 0
invalid move: rejected

steps.why: Constructing commands stores requests without executing them.
The old position is captured just before the setter call.
The second command sees the result of the first.

steps.state: Undo second: marker=3; undo first: marker=0.
steps.why: History is reversed from its newest change to its oldest.
The setter throws before assignment; failed work cannot be undone.

workshop.pitfall: Capture before_ in the constructor. Both queued moves may save zero, so undoing the second jumps from seven directly to zero instead of three. Both objects are constructed before either action executes.

discussion.question: Choose a saved old value or an inverse subtraction for a command that sets a marker to an absolute destination.
discussion.answer: Save the old value. Subtracting the destination after setting it always gives zero and cannot recover an arbitrary previous position. An inverse delta can work for bounded relative moves under the same isolation contract.
discussion.hint: Setting seven is not the same request as adding seven.

workshop.alternative: A vector of integers with a loop is sufficient for a fixed set of move-only requests. A std::function<void()> queue is compact for delayed work, but an undo contract still needs saved state and pairing between forward and reverse behavior.
workshop.design: Move holds the receiver, destination, prior position, and an applied flag. The queue owns commands but borrows no internal marker storage. Receiver validation happens before the command commits success.
invariants: The marker stays within its allowed range.
Only successful executions set applied_ true.
Commands must not outlive their borrowed receiver.
Undo history assumes no unrelated edits to the receiver.
workshop.maintenance: Representing requests explicitly gives a debugger a concrete place to inspect their arguments and state. Keep the history owner responsible for ordering and receiver lifetime instead of scattering undo calls across user-interface components.
workshop.verification: Checks cover delayed execution, the final queue value, repeated execution rejection, reverse undo, invalid destination, undo of a failed command, the upper boundary, and execute-after-undo. They do not establish persistence, concurrency safety, or recovery from process failure.

lab.task: Add run_batch for fresh commands sharing an exclusively controlled Marker. Execute in order. On std::out_of_range, undo the successfully applied prefix in reverse order and return false. Return true on success, including an empty batch. Preserve all primary checks.
checks: Fresh batch [6,11] from zero fails and restores zero.
An empty batch succeeds and preserves five.
lab.answer: The solution maintains a count rather than assuming the failing command is undoable. It catches only the specified range failure; logic errors remain programming errors. Rollback depends on valid saved positions and no unrelated changes. A production transaction wrapper would need a policy for rollback failures and other receiver types.

overview.title: A queue owns requests; requests borrow the marker
overview.explanation: The ownership edge ends at Command because that is the queue element type. Actual owned objects are Move instances. The inheritance arrow points from Move toward its base. The dependency arrow is a borrowed reference: deleting a command must never delete the marker. The invoker role belongs to the execution loops over queue, not to std::vector itself; main also performs the separate client role when constructing commands.
